paras: The whipping of Tom Jefferson was an attack by a crowd of white citizens on a Black man at Graniteville, South Carolina, on the night of January 11, 1903. Jefferson, accused of assaulting a crippled white boy at Aiken, was given more than fifty lashes and ordered to leave the community. An Associated Press dispatch from Augusta carried the story to papers across the South and beyond, and a one-sentence version reached the Richmond Planet through a syndicated news digest.

According to the Augusta dispatch, Jefferson was accused of having "assaulted a crippled white boy" in Aiken on the night of Saturday, January 10. No report describes what the assault consisted of or names the boy, and a later South Carolina paragraph said instead that Jefferson had "whipped" him. Jefferson had been arrested at Aiken on Saturday afternoon but was released "upon his promise to leave town."

Learning that Jefferson would board a train at Graniteville, "white citizens of that place" met him there. They gave him "over fifty lashes," with an order to leave the community at once. The reports name none of the men involved and give no number for the crowd.
No arrest of anyone in the crowd, and no official inquiry, appears in the coverage, and nothing further was reported about Jefferson.

The story ran first on January 13 in the Savannah Morning News, the Americus Times-Recorder and the Paducah Sun, and the Raleigh News & Observer credited it to the Associated Press the next day. Every version repeated the accusation as fact, and headlines ranged from "Whipped a Negro" and "Lashed for Assaulting a Cripple" to the Paducah Sun's "Whip a Malicious Negro." South Carolina weeklies reprinted the dispatch through January 20, the Newberry Herald and News adding a subhead that Jefferson "had been Allowed to Go Scot Free."

The Anderson Intelligencer called the whippers "indignant citizens" and remarked that "it is not said what the indignant citizens did to the authorities who released him." A one-line digest version, saying Jefferson was "driven from the town," ran in papers in Delaware and Virginia.

The only Black-press notice was the same digest sentence in the Richmond Planet of January 17, printed without headline or comment. Where the white digests read "a crippled white boy," the Planet's text read only "a crippled boy."

Most versions of the Augusta dispatch, dated January 12, placed the whipping "last night," but the Pickens People's Journal said "Monday night," which the dateline does not allow. The nature of the accusation also varied, from "assaulted" in the wire to "whipped" in the Anderson paragraph.

accounts.label: Augusta wire (Associated Press)
accounts.gist: Jefferson, who 'assaulted a crippled white boy' at Aiken on Saturday night, was arrested and released on a promise to leave; Graniteville citizens, learning he would take a train there, met him, gave him over fifty lashes and ordered him to leave.

accounts.label: Syndicated news digest
accounts.gist: One sentence: for assaulting a crippled boy at Aiken, Tom Jefferson, a negro, was whipped by a crowd of white people and driven from the town.

accounts.label: Anderson Intelligencer state news
accounts.gist: An unnamed negro who 'whipped' a little crippled white boy at Aiken and was released on a promise to leave was caught by 'indignant citizens' and 'severely thrashed'.

framing.detail: Most papers ran the Augusta dispatch under plain headlines such as 'Whipped a Negro' and 'Whipped and Ordered to Leave', stating the assault as fact.
The Newberry subhead said he 'had been Allowed to Go Scot Free', and the Anderson paragraph called the whippers 'indignant citizens' and turned its criticism on the authorities who released him.
The Richmond Planet printed only the syndicated digest sentence, without headline or comment, and its text reads 'a crippled boy' where the white digests read 'a crippled white boy'.

versions.value: 'Last night' in a dispatch dated Jan. 12, i.e. Jan. 11

conflicts.note: The Jan. 12 dateline cannot report a Monday-night event as past; the Pickens paper appears to have reworded 'last night', so Jan. 11 is better supported.
Neither version describes what happened; the Anderson paragraph is a later rewrite and gives no source.

versions.value: Whipped at Graniteville while leaving by train

conflicts.note: The digest compresses the wire; the fuller dispatch places the whipping at Graniteville.

Whipping ('over fifty lashes') and an order to leave; 'beating' rests only on the Anderson paper's 'severely thrashed', which describes the same whipping.

record_check.dossier: The wire says 'assaulted a crippled white boy'; 'whipped' appears only in the later Anderson rewrite.
One Black-press digest item and ten white printings (six of the full wire, three digest one-liners, one state-news rewrite).
Widely reprinted but resting on a single Augusta dispatch; no independent local report found.

info: Whipped Sunday night, Jan. 11, 1903 ('last night' in a Jan. 12 dispatch); one reprint says 'Monday night' (Jan. 12).
Whipped at Graniteville, S.C., where he was to board a train; the alleged assault, arrest and release were at Aiken, S.C.
Accused of having 'assaulted a crippled white boy' in Aiken on Saturday night, Jan. 10; the Anderson paper says he 'whipped' the boy. The nature of the act is not described.
'A crowd of white people' / 'white citizens' of Graniteville; 'indignant citizens' in the Anderson paper. None named.
